title: English 101: first-year composition
summary: Students write four essays through drafts, peer review and revision: a personal narrative, a rhetorical analysis, an argument with sources, and a researched essay in MLA style. The course builds from storytelling to analysis, argument and research. Short in-class writing and peer review run throughout.
brief: First-year composition (English 101) at a community college: 15 weeks, two 75-minute class meetings a week, 22 students. Students write four essays through drafts: a personal narrative, a rhetorical analysis, an argument with sources, and a researched essay with MLA citation; each has a draft, an in-class peer review and a revision. No textbook; I supply the readings. Four essays 15%, 20%, 20% and 25%, peer review participation 10%, short in-class writing 10%.
setup: No textbook; the instructor supplies the readings

l_b39c359102a4.title: Finding a story: freewriting and choosing a moment
l_b39c359102a4.summary: Students use freewriting, listing and mapping to find a single meaningful moment, and test it against what a reader needs to feel its stakes.

segments.title: Topic or moment?
segments.description:
Show the two pairs of phrases. Students jot a few words for each pair, naming which phrase is a bounded moment and why, for about one minute each.
They compare answers with a partner for one minute. Hear one.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: the second phrase in each pair. It names a particular time and action. The first phrase names a broad topic rather than a particular event. Link back to the star each student placed on the Hughes chapter last time. Keep it to a few words per pair.
shown: Pair 1: My summer job | The afternoon the freezer door locked behind me
Pair 2: My grandfather | The night my grandfather asked me to read his mail aloud

segments.title: Three ways to find a moment
segments.description:
Explain freewriting: write without stopping, without editing, and follow whatever comes. Explain listing: many short entries, each with a place and a rough date. Explain mapping: put one candidate at the center and branch out to people, place, action and feeling.
Draw a sample map on the board for a hypothetical moment: “the day the bus left without me”. Branches: driver, bus stop at 6:40 a.m., I ran and missed it, embarrassed and angry.
Before moving on, each student writes one sentence predicting which of the three will be hardest for them, and tells a partner.
segments.teacherNotes: Do not model with a topic any student might choose. Stress that freewriting is not graded for correctness and that spelling does not matter. Hughes can be the example: his map would branch from the bench in the church.
shown: Table: Method | What you do | What it gives you / Freewriting | Write without stopping | Unexpected memories and details / Listing | Many short entries with place and date | Many options quickly / Mapping | Branch out from one moment | Who, where, what happened, what you felt

segments.title: Freewrite from prompts
segments.description:
Show the four prompts. Students pick one and freewrite for four minutes without lifting the pen.
In the last minute they underline up to three different moments from their freewrite, each one a possible narrative topic.
Circulate and give no feedback.
segments.teacherNotes: If a student stalls, tell them to write “I can’t think” until something comes. Some memories may be painful. Remind students they choose what to write about and share only what they are comfortable sharing. Students who underline fewer than three can add more in the next segment by jotting a line on a second prompt.
shown: A time I had to decide something quickly
A time I was embarrassed in front of other people
A time I changed my mind about someone
A place or a moment I would go back to if I could

segments.title: List, then map three candidates
segments.description:
Hand out the sheet "Moment list and three maps". In Part 1, students list the moments they underlined in their freewrite, plus any others it brings to mind. They have two minutes and write at least five entries, each with a moment and its setting: the place and a rough date or time of year.
In Part 2, they circle three entries that could each be a single scene, for one minute.
For each circled entry, they sketch a quick map for about a minute and a half, with a few words under Who, Where, What and Felt.
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: listing periods such as “high school” or “my divorce”. Ask: Could you stand in the room where it happened? Students with few ideas can return to another prompt and add a line. Keep map boxes to a few words each. The sheet holds all three maps on one page; tell students to keep it, since they need it later in the lesson and next time.

segments.title: Testing a moment for stakes
segments.description:
Show the four questions of the moment test. Talk through them using the Hughes bench as the example: one evening, two kinds of loss, a scene a reader can see.
Students silently mark which of their three candidates passes the most questions.
segments.teacherNotes: Stakes were named last time: what the narrator stands to gain or lose. Expect the answer “nothing was at stake, it was just funny”. Ask what the person risked, such as pride, a friendship or being believed.
shown: Steps: Is it one bounded moment? → Is something at stake for the narrator? → Can I picture it in detail? → Can a reader who was not there feel why it mattered?

segments.title: Find the problem, then choose
segments.description:
Show a hypothetical justification a student might write. Students decide in writing which test question it fails and rewrite it in two sentences so it names a bounded moment and what was at stake.
Partners compare rewrites for one minute. Each student then stars one of their own three moments for the test.
segments.teacherNotes: The flawed statement announces a lesson and covers a whole period. Sample rewrite: “On the driveway the night before my road test, I admitted to Dad that I had failed once already, and I risked his trust.” Watch for rewrites that still state the lesson.
shown: Hypothetical justification: “I chose the summer I learned to drive because it taught me independence and responsibility, and it was an important time in my life.”

segments.title: Short in-class writing: why this moment matters
segments.description:
Direct students to its scoring instructions, then show the prompt. Students write alone for six minutes, in about six sentences.
They write on the moment they starred, and keep the paragraph for the next segment. Circulate and give no feedback during writing.
segments.teacherNotes: Strong response: names the moment in one sentence, states what the narrator could gain or lose, and includes one concrete detail. Weak response: describes a period or says only that it was important. This is the short in-class writing component and is done in class.
shown: Prompt: Which moment did you choose, and why does it matter? Name the moment, say what you stood to gain or lose, and include one detail a reader could see or hear.

segments.title: Peer review: exchange and read
segments.description:
Hand out copies of the full Peer review participation brief and its accompanying rubric again, with this meeting’s questions printed with the piece. Identify Peer review participation as 10% of the course grade. Students exchange paragraphs with their partner and read the partner’s paragraph for three minutes.
They then write responses to the three questions shown, for five minutes, referring to the writer’s exact words.
segments.teacherNotes: This peer review participation is scored as it happens with the rubric accompanying the brief. Questions and sample answers: 1, a copied phrase such as “I had never lied to him before” plus how it shaped the reader’s sense of why the moment matters; if no stake appears, name what stays unclear, e.g. what the writer risked. 2, one moment or a longer period, with a reason supported by the wording. 3, a real question, e.g. “What did he say next?” Weak: “Good job.”

segments.title: Peer review: responses aloud and one change
segments.description:
Pair by pair around the room, each student gives the writer their responses aloud in about one minute. They give their answer to question 1 with the quoted wording, then ask the reader’s question from question 3. The writer listens.
The class listens quietly while you score each student as it happens. In the last minute, each writer writes one change they would make to their own paragraph.
segments.teacherNotes: Eleven pairs, about two minutes a pair including the move. Seat pairs side by side. Use a seating chart for all 22 and score each student during their own turn with the brief’s rubric. Each turn is about one minute; question 2 stays on the page. Cut a turn at one minute so the round fits.

segments.title: What comes next
segments.description:
Tell students that next time they will practice showing rather than telling, using sensory detail and dialogue to build a scene. They will then plan the first draft of Essay 1.
Tell them the practice quiz on today’s lesson is for after class and counts toward no grade. Remind them to keep their three maps and starred moment.
segments.teacherNotes: Nothing needs bringing beyond something to write with and today’s maps. Ask students to keep the Essay 1 prompt where they can reach it.

keyIdeas: Freewriting, listing and mapping are three ways to find material. Each one produces candidate moments, and none of them produces a finished essay.
A narrative topic is not yet a moment. A moment is bounded in time and place: one afternoon, one conversation, one decision.
A moment is worth choosing when something is at stake in it and a reader who was not there can picture it and feel what the narrator stood to gain or lose.
Choosing is a decision that can be justified. Writers test several candidates against the same questions instead of taking the first idea.
Peer review depends on specific attention: quote the writer’s words, explain how you responded as a reader, and ask a real question.

vocabulary.definition: Writing without stopping or correcting to discover ideas and memories you did not plan to write about.
Making a fast list of short entries, such as moments with a place and a time, to see many options at once.
Sketching a candidate moment at the center with branches for people, place, action and feeling.
An event limited to one time and place, such as a single conversation or decision, as opposed to a long period.
One of several possible moments you are considering before you choose which to write about.
A short explanation of why you made a choice, naming what is at stake and what a reader can picture.

study.overview: Good personal narratives start with a moment, not a topic. This lesson gave you three ways to find material (freewriting, listing and mapping), a four-question test for choosing among your candidates, and a way to explain your choice. It also practiced peer review that points to a writer’s exact words. Use this guide to review the methods and to check the moment you starred before you plan your draft.

points.heading: Freewriting, listing and mapping each find material
points.explanation: Freewriting means writing without stopping or editing and following whatever memory comes. Spelling does not matter. If you stall, write “I can’t think” until something arrives. Listing means making many short entries, each with a place and a rough date or time of year. It gives you many options quickly. Mapping means putting one candidate at the center and branching out to who, where, what happened and what you felt. Suppose a map for “the day the bus left without me” has these branches: the driver, the bus stop at 6:40 a.m., I ran and missed it, embarrassed and angry. In a few words the map shows a person, a place, an action and a feeling. None of these methods produces a finished essay. Each one produces candidates for you to test.

points.heading: A topic is not yet a moment
points.explanation: A moment is bounded in time and place: one afternoon, one conversation, one decision. A topic covers a broad stretch. Compare “My summer job” with “The afternoon the freezer door locked behind me.” Compare “My grandfather” with “The night my grandfather asked me to read his mail aloud.” The second phrase in each pair names a particular time and action. The first names a subject you could write about for years. One check is to ask whether you could stand in the room where it happened. You can stand in a driveway on a particular night. You cannot stand in “high school.” Adding more description to a broad topic does not make it a moment. You have to narrow it to one event.

points.heading: Test each candidate for stakes, then justify your choice
points.explanation: Run each candidate through the same four questions. Is it one bounded moment? Is something at stake for the narrator? Can I picture it in detail? Can a reader who was not there feel why it mattered? Stakes are what the narrator stood to gain or lose, such as pride, a friendship or being believed. A moment can be funny and still have stakes if the person risked something. Your justification should name the moment and the stakes instead of announcing a lesson. Suppose a student wrote, “I chose the summer I learned to drive because it taught me independence and responsibility.” That covers a whole season and states a lesson. A stronger version might read: “On the driveway the night before my road test, I admitted to Dad that I had failed once already, and I risked his trust.” It names one scene, one action and one risk.

points.heading: Peer review depends on specific attention
points.explanation: Useful feedback points to the writer’s exact words so the writer can find what you mean. Then it explains how you responded as a reader, and it asks a real question. Suppose a paragraph includes the sentence “I had never lied to him before.” A strong reader copies that phrase and explains that it made her see the trust the writer might lose. If no stake appears, the reader names what stays unclear, such as what the writer risked. A real question might be “What did he say next?” A comment like “Good job” gives the writer nothing to act on. Peer review participation is 10% of the course grade, so practice these three moves each time you read a partner’s writing. After you hear feedback on your own work, decide on one change you would make.

values.text: Folio could not fix this itself: Counted by its parts this needs about 8 minutes and has 5: 1 × Freewrite on a chosen prompt (5 min), 3 × Identify up to three candidate moments (3 min). Cut a part of it, or give it more minutes.

t_a63a440ab2ed.title: Peer review participation
t_a63a440ab2ed.prompt: Peer review participation is 10% of the course grade. Give your partner feedback that helps them decide what to revise. Use the questions handed out or shown at that meeting to guide your response. Your work is scored individually as you give your feedback aloud, using the rubric below. Each criterion earns 1–4 points, for a total of 12 points per scored meeting. Scored meetings count equally toward this component.
steps: Keep this brief in front of you. Exchange the writing specified at the meeting with your partner, and read your partner’s writing carefully.
Write responses to the questions handed out or shown at that meeting. Refer to specific wording or passages so the writer can locate what you discuss.
When your turn is called, give your responses aloud to the writer. Explain your observations and ask your reader’s question. Listen while your partner gives feedback on your writing.
After hearing your partner’s feedback, write one change you would make to your own writing.
t_a63a440ab2ed.answerKey:
1. Allow partners to exchange and read the writing during the reading period specified for the meeting. Keep copies of this brief in students’ hands.
2. Allow the response-writing period specified for the meeting. Responses depend on each partner’s writing; there is no single correct answer. Written responses support the oral feedback.
3. Call pairs in seating order and hear each partner separately. Other students listen while the instructor scores the speaker’s oral feedback against all rubric criteria. Record individual criterion scores as the feedback occurs. Maintain a running record identifying the meeting, scheduled speakers and scores; use the meeting’s designated group and speaking allocation to manage turns.
4. Allow writers to note a revision after hearing their partners. The revision note supports the writer’s next decision; the participation score comes from the feedback performed aloud.

t_a6fceec12d3a.title: Short in-class writing: Finding a story: freewriting and choosing a moment
t_a6fceec12d3a.prompt: Short in-class writing counts for 10% of the course grade. Each writing assignment counts equally toward that grade. Work alone for six minutes. Write one short paragraph of about three sentences about your starred moment. Your paragraph is scored out of 12 points using the rubric below.
steps: Name the moment you starred, including when and where it happened. Explain what you stood to gain or lose and include one detail a reader could see or hear. Use about three sentences to show why you chose this moment.
Keep your paragraph for the peer review activity that follows.
t_a6fceec12d3a.answerKey:
1. Direct all 22 students to read the scoring instructions, then write independently during the same six-minute interval. Allow roughly four minutes for the short paragraph and the remaining time to finish and reread. Circulate without giving feedback. There is no single correct response: assess the student’s chosen moment using the rubric. After class, award 1–4 points for each criterion and total the scores out of 12.
2. Students keep their paragraphs available for the peer review activity that immediately follows. Keeping the paragraph earns no separate points.

descriptors.x_ed255aba4d11: Identifies precise wording or a passage and explains clearly what works for the reader.
descriptors.x_f20f3d7031f4: Identifies relevant wording or a passage and names what works for the reader.
descriptors.x_3203b954bdef: Refers to the writing generally, with limited explanation of what works.
descriptors.x_40a41691e61f: Offers general praise or criticism without locating support in the writing.

descriptors.x_ed255aba4d11: Answers the meeting’s review questions directly and supports observations with clear reasons grounded in the writing.
descriptors.x_f20f3d7031f4: Answers the meeting’s review questions and gives relevant reasons for observations.
descriptors.x_3203b954bdef: Answers the review questions partly or gives reasons that are vague or weakly connected to the writing.
descriptors.x_40a41691e61f: Leaves the review questions largely unanswered or gives judgments without reasons.

descriptors.x_ed255aba4d11: Asks a specific, open question that identifies an unresolved reader concern and gives the writer a clear direction for reconsidering the writing.
descriptors.x_f20f3d7031f4: Asks a relevant question that helps the writer consider a possible revision.
descriptors.x_3203b954bdef: Asks a broad or partly relevant question whose value for revision is unclear.
descriptors.x_40a41691e61f: Provides no genuine reader question or asks a question unrelated to the writing.
